analysis.one_liner: Expands affordable housing aid and down-payment grants, paid for by raising the estate tax on large estates.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 11, 2025 with 26 cosponsors, referred to four House committees, and has received no markup or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would spend large sums on housing: grants to state and local governments to loosen zoning rules, roughly $48 billion a year for the federal affordable-housing trust fund, $70 billion for public housing repairs, and down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value for first-time homebuyers whose parents never owned a home. It would also strengthen fair-housing and tenant protections, tighten lending rules on banks and nonbank mortgage companies, and pay for part of it by raising the estate tax on the largest estates. It has not moved in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters, first-time homebuyers whose parents did not own a home (grants up to 3.5% of a home's value), borrowers who owe more than their homes are worth, tenants facing eviction or harassment, rural and tribal households, and homebuyers protected by expanded fair-housing rules covering sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, source of income, and veteran status [S2][S3]. Construction workers benefit from prevailing-wage requirements on funded projects [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $2 billion a year (2025-2029) in competitive grants to state, local, and tribal governments that cut zoning barriers, allow denser housing and accessory units, and adopt tenant protections like just-cause eviction and access to counsel in eviction cases [S3].

Authorizes $48 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund and $3 billion a year for the Capital Magnet Fund through 2034, $70 billion for the public housing capital fund in 2025, and a $4 billion Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund, with new units required to stay affordable in perpetuity and built at prevailing wages [S3].

Creates down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's appraised value for first-time homebuyers who are also first-generation buyers earning under 120% of area median income, funded through 2034 [S3].
Authorizes $5 billion to help borrowers with negative equity pay arrears, liens, and repairs in neighborhoods where homes are worth less than the cost to build [S3].
Expands the Fair Housing Act to ban discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, source of income, veteran status, or perceived membership in a protected class [S2].

Restricts FHA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac sales of foreclosed properties and distressed loans: at least 75% of FHA foreclosed homes must go to owner-occupants or nonprofits, borrowers must get 90 days' notice before a loan sale, and buyers must offer loss mitigation at least as good as before the sale [S3].

Strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act by covering nonbank mortgage companies, requiring community benefits plans for merger approvals, and imposing penalties for repeated failing grades, including clawing back executive compensation [S3].

Raises revenue by reducing the estate tax to three brackets with higher rates and a lower basic exemption, adding a surcharge on high-income estates, and tightening trust and valuation rules used to shrink taxable estates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The largest estates, through higher estate tax rates, a smaller exemption, a surtax on high-income estates, and new limits on trusts and valuation discounts used to avoid the tax [S2][S3]. The general Treasury also funds the housing appropriations [S3]. Large banks, nonbank mortgage companies, mortgage servicers, and investors in distressed loans bear new examination, compliance, and penalty exposure [S3]. Landlords and investors face tenant-protection incentives and limits on reselling foreclosed FHA-backed homes [S3].

drawbacks.text: The authorized spending is very large: $48 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund and $3 billion a year for the Capital Magnet Fund through 2034 alone, plus $70 billion for public housing in 2025, $5 billion for appraisal-gap grants, and $2 billion a year in local grants, with the estate-tax changes covering only part of it, so the rest adds to the deficit unless other revenue is found [S3].

Eligibility for the down-payment program rests on borrower self-attestation, and the bill bars creditors from liability or repurchase requirements when they rely on those attestations in good faith, which weakens the main check against false claims [S3].

Down-payment grants add buyer purchasing power; if housing supply does not rise as fast as demand, some of the subsidy could be absorbed into higher home prices rather than lower costs for buyers [S3].

Stronger Community Reinvestment Act penalties, including restrictions on growth and executive compensation clawbacks, would fall on banks regardless of whether individual executives or frontline workers had any role in the shortfall [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and targeted at people priced out of housing: down-payment help, repaired public housing, permanent affordability requirements, and real tenant protections. The honest objections are fiscal and design-related: the spending is far larger than the estate-tax offset, self-attested eligibility with lender immunity invites abuse, and demand-side grants can inflate prices unless supply grows alongside them. On the merits it is a serious, expensive attempt at a problem most Americans feel directly; the record so far shows no attempt to pass it.

outcome.mechanism: It went to four House committees in March 2025 and to a Financial Services subcommittee two weeks later, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: Representative Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on March 11, 2025, with 26 Democratic cosponsors [S4][S5].
The same day, it was referred to four committees: Financial Services, plus the Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means committees [S5].
On March 27, 2025, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, where it has remained [S5].
No committee has held a markup or vote, and no chamber has voted on it; the 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the groups the bill would tax or regulate — the largest estates, large banks, and nonbank mortgage companies — are untouched because no chamber has voted; renters and aspiring homebuyers have gained nothing yet either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks and large estates, so far

sides.party_line_note: All 27 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; the bill sits in committees controlled by the 223-seat Republican majority and has drawn no Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill raises estate tax rates, lowers the exemption, adds a surcharge on high-income estates, and closes trust and valuation strategies used to avoid the tax. Its interest in blocking the bill runs directly against the funding for housing it would pay for.

The Community Reinvestment Act rewrite extends exams, requires community benefits plans for mergers, deducts fossil-fuel expansion lending from community-development credit, and imposes growth restrictions and executive pay clawbacks for repeated failing grades. Banks' interest in avoiding these obligations runs against communities' access to credit.
For the first time they would be examined under the Community Reinvestment Act like depository banks. Their interest in staying unexamined runs against the borrowers they serve.

The bill restricts sales of FHA, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac distressed loans, requires 90-day borrower notice and loss mitigation no worse than before the sale, and makes noncompliance a defense to foreclosure. Servicer and investor interest in reselling loans cheaply runs against homeowners behind on payments.

Grant incentives reward jurisdictions that adopt just-cause eviction, rent-stabilization measures, and anti-harassment enforcement, and the bill bars reselling FHA foreclosed homes through land contracts. Landlord interest in fewer tenant protections runs against tenants' security.

The Housing Trust Fund, Capital Magnet Fund, and Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund channel construction money through nonprofits and state housing agencies, and 'community partners' get priority to buy HUD and enterprise foreclosure properties.
More funded construction means more work, with prevailing-wage requirements attached to federally financed projects, and the zoning-reform grants aim to make building denser housing easier.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, referral to four committees, and a large estate-tax increase at its core, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in the 119th Congress. The realistic path is that it dies in committee at the end of the session unless housing becomes a negotiating priority in a must-pass bill.
